newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bank Austria sets sights on expansion.
newsitem.headline: Bank Austria sets sights on expansion.

text.p: When Austria conceived the privatisation of blue-blooded Creditanstalt-Bankverein six years ago, new owner Bank Austria was not even born.
The nation's biggest bank grew out of the 1991 merger of leading savings bank Zentralsparkasse, controlled by the City of Vienna, and number four commercial bank Laenderbank, also partly state-owned.

Bank Austria started life as market leader and chief executive Gerhard Randa put that position beyond all doubt on Sunday when he finally won the race to buy the government's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt.

The marriage of Austria's first and second banks will create a financial institution to rank among Europe's top 30 and dominate the domestic scene, with a market share of 25 percent in asset terms, 70 percent of commercial banking, 80 percent of Vienna bourse trade and half of export financing.
The union may also mark the beginning of the end for Austria's "proporz" system that carves up the economy along party political lines.
Bank Austria has its roots deep in social democracy while Creditanstalt wears its conservatism like a badge.

Bank Austria's political colours are reflected in its ownership structure. The Social Democrat-ruled City of Vienna effectively holds 46 percent of voting shares, or roughly 40 percent of equity, through its foundation Anteilsverwaltung Zentralsparkasse (AVZ).
As a result Vienna guarantees the bank's existing and future liabilities, ensuring an AAA rating.
The Republic of Austria controls 20 percent of voting shares, or around 17 percent of equity, making it the second biggest single shareholder.
Germany's WestLB acquired 10.3 percent of ordinary stock, or 9.1 percent of total equity, at the start of 1996. Italy's Cariplo has around 4.5 percent of ordinary shares, or 3.9 percent of equity.
At the end of 1995 Bank Austria had total assets of almost 688 billion schillings ($62.04 billion), giving it a 12.8 percent market share.
Since taking over as chief executive in 1995, Randa has tried to put the focus on core business and reduce the bank's industrial holdings.

Nevertheless, Bank Austria still has a huge network of non-financial interests ranging from a 30 percent stake in listed fibre maker Lenzing to a majority stake in porcelain maker Wiener Porzellanmanufaktur.

It also has ties to construction firms. It owns 33 percent of listed Allgemeine Baugesellschaft A Porr AG, 100 percent of unlisted Wiener Betriebs und Baugesellscahft m. b. H. and a minority stake in STUAG Bau AG.
In all, Bank Austria has fingers in 189 industrial companies, of which 41 are in the property business.

According to a recent report by Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the two principal investments in terms of size are tourism firms Oesterreichisches Verkehrsbuero, estimated at two billion, and Wigast AG, one billion.

Bank Austria has had at times an uneasy relationship with the nation's third biggest bank GiroCredit, majority-owned by AVZ. The two cooperate in areas like investment banking but operate independent commercial and savings businesses. ($1=11.09 Schilling)
